tldr: This is a loose research thread on agent security, not one event. It opened with an arXiv paper arguing that coding harnesses wired to shells, filesystems, and sockets become Living-off-the-Land platforms once an injected instruction lands.
whats_new: A Nov 19 audit questions whether AI-agent security benchmarks score attacks correctly, asking if reported "attack succeeded" verdicts actually hold up.
why_it_matters: If benchmark verdicts on agent attacks are unreliable, the security scores you use to pick a harness or guardrail may not reflect real exposure.

beats.headline: Coding harnesses framed as Living-off-the-Land attack platforms
beats.summary: Paper maps prompt injection through retrieved content to shell, file, and network actions, and proposes compositional defenses.

beats.headline: Practitioner take on old failures, plus an audit of benchmark verdicts
beats.summary: Attention shifts from attack surface to whether the measurements of attack success can be trusted.

open_questions: Which named agent-security benchmarks does the verdict audit find mis-scoring attacks, and in which direction?
Do benchmark maintainers publish corrected verdicts or revised scoring rules?
Does the compositional defense architecture get an implementation or evaluation against a real harness?
take_for_builders: Before trusting an agent-security benchmark score, spot-check a sample of its "attack succeeded" and "attack failed" verdicts against the raw transcripts.

day_captions.1b66b3acc2678fad: Practitioner view that AI security repeats familiar failure classes through new attack paths.
day_captions.cd759e6684ea23fc: Moves the thread to measurement: audits whether benchmark attack-success verdicts are correct.
